**The Quiet Rebellion of Small Things**

I’ve been thinking about how the most revolutionary acts in 2024 all look suspiciously like boredom.

While the timeline screams at us in 280-character increments, there’s a silent mutiny happening in living rooms and late-night kitchens. People are choosing to read physical books again. Not as performance, not for the ‘gram, but because they want the particular smell of old paper and the way the spine fights back when you open it too wide.

I keep seeing houseplants thriving in apartments that used to be shrines to minimalism. Actual dirt. Actual neglect followed by sudden, desperate research at 2 a.m. about “why is my monstera crying.” There’s something almost defiant about deciding that caring for something slower than the internet is a worthy use of your finite heartbeats.

The other day I watched a grown man spend twenty minutes trying to get the perfect pour on his coffee while his phone sat in another room. He looked like a monk performing a tea ceremony. I don’t think he even realized he was smiling.

We’re in the middle of the biggest attention economy heist in human history, and some of us are choosing to be bad at being robbed.

There’s a peculiar dignity in becoming slightly unreachable. In saying, without saying it, *I have things worth protecting from the noise.* Not out of superiority. Just out of a bone-deep exhaustion with performing thought instead of having it.

The revolution won’t be livestreamed. It’ll be someone closing their laptop at 8 p.m. and going outside to watch the sky do its ancient, indifferent thing. It’ll be choosing to remember what your own thoughts sound like when they’re not being interrupted by push notifications about other people’s thoughts.

The world is on fire in seventeen different ways, and yet my neighbor just spent all weekend building an absurdly over-engineered birdhouse. I respect that man more than most CEOs.

Maybe the real flex isn’t keeping up anymore.

Maybe it’s opting out so thoroughly, so joyfully, that you become a kind of living proof that another tempo is still possible. That the machine hasn’t won yet. That somewhere, in some unmonetized corner of existence, a human is still allowed to be slow, and strange, and genuinely preoccupied with whether their sourdough starter is happy.

I think that’s worth writing about.
